archetypes.pain: "I wait days for someone to run a query for me." / "I can't write SQL." / "Every question becomes a ticket."

archetypes.needs: a folder of PDFs, Word docs or web pages.

archetypes.needs: a sample of the form, ideally 10+ of the same layout.

archetypes.prompt_skeleton: extract `<their fields>` from the documents in my stage into a table, and keep it current as new files land.
archetypes.what_gets_built: a pipeline turning a stage of documents into a clean table.

archetypes.needs: a table with a free-text column.
archetypes.pain: "Too much comes in to sort by hand." / "We read every complaint to find the urgent ones."
archetypes.prompt_skeleton: classify `<their text column>` into `<their categories>`, score sentiment, and surface the ones needing attention first.
archetypes.what_gets_built: classification and sentiment over a backlog, with a triage view.

archetypes.what_gets_built: a Cortex Agent with tools that completes a multi-step task.

archetypes.needs: a time series - a date column and a value column, ideally 12+ months.

archetypes.needs: two or more sources that share a key.

routes.guidance: Openflow has a first-party connector for Azure Blob Storage and SQL Server. For Fabric or OneLake, register the Iceberg tables through a catalog integration and query them in place - no copy.
Point an external stage at the S3 bucket with a storage integration, then Snowpipe for continuous load. If the data is already Iceberg in Glue, use a catalog integration and leave it where it is.
A storage integration over the GCS bucket plus an external stage. BigQuery data moves cleanly as Parquet exported to GCS, or through Openflow if you need it on a schedule.
Openflow's Oracle connector does change data capture, so you get an ongoing replica rather than a nightly dump. Start with the handful of tables the proof of concept actually reads.
Either the SAP connector for Snowflake, or SAP Business Data Cloud sharing the data as Iceberg that Snowflake reads without a copy. The second route is usually faster to stand up.
Openflow can run inside your network and push out, so nothing has to be exposed inbound. For a first proof of concept, a one-off bulk load of a representative extract is usually enough.
Openflow has connectors for the common SaaS sources, and the Marketplace carries some of them as ready-made shares. Check the Marketplace first - it is the cheaper answer when it exists.
Nothing to move. Point the proof of concept at the existing tables and spend the saved time on the model and the interface instead.
Worth ten minutes with whoever owns the source before you build. The answer changes the effort more than any other decision here.
